parsed.hook: Woodruff Vineyard sits on a 1,200-foot ridge where fractured shale and sandstone force Pinot Noir vines to dig deep, yielding fruit with a mineral edge rare in California. Wind Gap’s 2013 and 2014 bottlings prove this site can deliver Burgundian tension without sacrificing New World ripeness—if you’re willing to pay the Santa Cruz Mountains premium.
parsed.wine_summary: Wind Gap’s Woodruff Vineyard Pinot Noir is a study in how elevation and geology can outmaneuver California’s warmth. The vineyard clings to a steep, west-facing slope in the Santa Cruz Mountains’ upper reaches, where afternoon fog from the Pacific lingers until noon, then burns off to reveal intense sun. This diurnal swing—often 30°F or more—preserves acidity while allowing full phenolic ripeness, a balance that eludes most coastal Pinot sites. Winemaker Pax Mahle’s minimalist approach (native yeast, neutral oak, no fining) lets the site speak: these wines taste like crushed rocks and wild cherries, not jam or oak spice. The producer’s reputation for Syrah and Chardonnay overshadows their Pinot, but Woodruff is the sleeper hit—small lots (under 200 cases per vintage) that reward those who track them down.
parsed.terroir_expression: The vineyard’s shale and sandstone soils—part of the Franciscan Complex, a chaotic mix of ancient seabed and volcanic debris—drain so aggressively that vines struggle to retain water, stressing them into concentration. The iron-rich red soils add a ferrous note to the wine’s mid-palate, while the elevation (1,200 feet) keeps alcohol in check (13.5% in 2013, 13.8% in 2014). The Pacific’s influence is palpable: a saline tang on the finish, like biting into a just-ripe plum near the ocean. Unlike the lush, fruit-forward Pinots of the Russian River Valley, Woodruff’s wines taste leaner, with a stony austerity that recalls the Côte de Nuits—but with California’s sun-drenched fruit density.
parsed.vinification_summary: Pax Mahle ferments the wine in open-top concrete tanks with native yeasts, a choice that amplifies the vineyard’s mineral character by avoiding the vanilla and spice notes of new oak. The wine sees 12–18 months in neutral French oak barrels, which soften tannins without imparting flavor. Mahle avoids fining or filtration, so the wine retains a slight textural grip—think of it as the difference between a polished river stone and one still rough from the creek. This hands-off approach means vintage variation is real: the 2013 (cooler, with higher acidity) feels more angular, while the 2014 (warmer, with riper tannins) drinks broader but still nervy.
